$ xref c

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. Decompile a function

Decompile functions to structured, typed pseudo-C. c lifts the machine code of each function containing the given addresses: arguments, local variables, loops and branches, calls with their constant arguments, and string literals.

Use it to read what a function does after you found it with refs, callers or field. Alias: decomp.

Usage

xref c [OPTIONS] <ADDRS>...

Each address may point anywhere inside a function; the whole function (its exact .eh_frame range) is decompiled.

Arguments and options

Arguments

<ADDRS>...
Addresses inside the functions to decompile.

Options

--from <FROM>
First address to print.
--to <TO>
End address (exclusive).
--out <OUT>
Write each decompiled function to <OUT>/<start>.c in parallel and print path, size and elapsed time.
--fields
Rewrite raw pointer offsets as inferred ->f_<off> field hints using layout recovery.
--goto
Keep residual labels and gotos instead of introducing skip flags; retain structured loops and branches.
--only-paths-to <ADDR>
Emit only basic blocks that can reach this instruction address.

Examples

The examples use the official ripgrep 14.1.1 release binary and its statistics serializer at 0x1835f0 (see field).

Decompile a function

Command
$ xref -b rg c 0x1835f0
Output
/*
 * fn_1835f0 — 0x1835f0..0x18374c (348 bytes, 1 direct caller; synthetic FDE entry)
 *   params:
 *     arg_0 (rdi): unk64 — 64-bit register (signedness unconstrained)
 *     arg_1 (rsi): void * — dereferenced by store
 *   return: unk64 in rax (consumed by 1/1 direct call site)
 */
unk64 fn_1835f0(unk64 arg_0, void *arg_1) {
  void *ptr_1 = arg_1; /* rsi */
  void *slot_0; /* [rsp+0x0], addr-taken */
  u32 slot_8; /* [rsp+0x8] */

  void *ptr_2 = *(u64 *)(ptr_1);
  *(u64 *)(ptr_1 + 24) = (*(u64 *)(ptr_1 + 24) + 1);
  *(u8 *)(ptr_1 + 32) = 0;
  usize v_3 = *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24);
  if (*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 8) == v_3) {
    void *v_5 = ptr_1;
    /* fn_80aa0: calls fn_80b3b, fn_12a6d0 */
    fn_80aa0(ptr_2 + 8, v_3, 1, 1, 1);
    ptr_1 = v_5;
    v_3 = *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24);
  }
  ((u8 *)*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 16))[v_3] = 123;
  *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24) = (v_3 + 1);
  *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 32) = (*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 32) + 1);
  slot_0 = ptr_1;
  slot_8 = 1;
  /* fn_15bf60: calls fn_15bfdc, fn_15c049, fn_80aa0 */
  unk64 v_4 = fn_15bf60(&slot_0, "elapsed", 7, arg_0 + 48);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches", 8, arg_0);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches_with_match", 19, arg_0 + 8);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "bytes_searched", 14, arg_0 + 16);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "bytes_printed", 13, arg_0 + 24);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "matched_lines", 13, arg_0 + 32);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    return v_4;
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "matches", 7, (arg_0 + 40));
  if (v_4 == 0) {
    /* fn_187760: writes arg_0 (+0x18); calls fn_187806, fn_80aa0, fn_1877e0 */
    v_4 = fn_187760(slot_0, slot_8);
  }
  return v_4;
}
stderr
xref: load 2.4ms, total 8.9ms

How to read it:

  • The header comment gives the function range and size, how many direct callers it has, and the inferred signature: arg_0 (rdi), arg_1 (rsi) with a type where the code constrains it (void * when it is dereferenced, unk64 when nothing is known) and the return register.
  • ptr_*, v_* are values held in registers; slot_* are stack slots (addr-taken when their address escapes, as &slot_0 does here).
  • A comment above each call names what the callee itself calls (/* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, … */), so you can tell helpers apart without opening them.
  • String arguments are shown as literals with their length: fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches", 8, arg_0) is a call (state, key, key_len, &value). The pairs "searches"/arg_0, "searches_with_match"/arg_0 + 8, … give the field layout directly.
  • ((u8 *)…)[v_3] = 123; writes { (123) into an output buffer: this is a JSON writer opening an object.

Field hints

Command
$ xref -b rg c 0x1835f0 --fields
Output
/* field offsets: arg_0 [+0x8:addr, +0x10:addr, +0x18:addr, +0x20:addr, +0x28:addr]; arg_1 [+0x0:u64, +0x18:u64, +0x20:u8] */
/*
 * fn_1835f0 — 0x1835f0..0x18374c (348 bytes, 1 direct caller; synthetic FDE entry)
 *   params:
 *     arg_0 (rdi): unk64 — 64-bit register (signedness unconstrained)
 *     arg_1 (rsi): void * — dereferenced by store
 *   return: unk64 in rax (consumed by 1/1 direct call site)
 */
unk64 fn_1835f0(unk64 arg_0, void *arg_1) {
  void *ptr_1 = arg_1; /* rsi */
  void *slot_0; /* [rsp+0x0], addr-taken */
  u32 slot_8; /* [rsp+0x8] */

  void *ptr_2 = *(u64 *)(ptr_1);
Output cut here: lines 1–14 of 67 shown.
stderr
xref: load 2.3ms, total 8.8ms

--fields adds a first line summarising the offsets each pointer argument is accessed at (arg_0 [+0x8:addr, …]; arg_1 [+0x0:u64, +0x18:u64, +0x20:u8]) and rewrites dereferences as ->f_<offset> hints where layout recovery is confident. addr means only the field's address is taken (passed on), never loaded, so this function's body is unchanged apart from the summary; in functions that load and store fields the body shows ptr->f_10 instead of *(u64 *)(ptr + 16).

Part of a function

Command
$ xref -b rg c 0x1835f0 --from 0x183644 --to 0x183690
Output
/*
 * fn_1835f0 — 0x1835f0..0x18374c (348 bytes, 1 direct caller; synthetic FDE entry)
 *   params:
 *     arg_0 (rdi): unk64 — 64-bit register (signedness unconstrained)
 *     arg_1 (rsi): void * — dereferenced by store
 *   return: unk64 in rax (consumed by 1/1 direct call site)
 */
unk64 fn_1835f0(unk64 arg_0, void *arg_1) {
  /* ... slice from 0x183644 (function starts at 0x1835f0) ... */
  unk64 v_8; /* rcx */
  unk64 v_9; /* rsi */
  unk64 v_10; /* rdi */
  u32 v_11; /* rdx */
  void *slot_0; /* [rsp+0x0], addr-taken */

  /* fn_15bf60: calls fn_15bfdc, fn_15c049, fn_80aa0 */
  unk64 v_4 = fn_15bf60(v_10, v_9, v_11, v_8);
  if (v_4 != 0) goto L_183717;
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches", 8, arg_0);
  if (v_4 != 0) goto L_183717;
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches_with_match", 19, arg_0 + 8);
  /* ... truncated at 0x183690 (function ends at 0x18374c) ... */
}
stderr
xref: load 2.6ms, total 9.3ms

--from/--to print only the statements for that address range, marked with slice from … / truncated at … comments. Registers live at the start of the range appear as fresh variables (v_8, v_10).

Only the paths that reach an instruction

Command
$ xref -b rg c 0x1835f0 --only-paths-to 0x183685
Output
/*
 * fn_1835f0 — 0x1835f0..0x18374c (348 bytes, 1 direct caller; synthetic FDE entry)
 *   params:
 *     arg_0 (rdi): unk64 — 64-bit register (signedness unconstrained)
 *     arg_1 (rsi): void * — dereferenced by store
 *   return: unk64 in rax (consumed by 1/1 direct call site)
 */
unk64 fn_1835f0(unk64 arg_0, void *arg_1) {
  void *ptr_1 = arg_1; /* rsi */
  void *slot_0; /* [rsp+0x0], addr-taken */
  u32 slot_8; /* [rsp+0x8] */

  void *ptr_2 = *(u64 *)(ptr_1);
  *(u64 *)(ptr_1 + 24) = (*(u64 *)(ptr_1 + 24) + 1);
  *(u8 *)(ptr_1 + 32) = 0;
  usize v_3 = *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24);
  if (*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 8) == v_3) {
    void *v_5 = ptr_1;
    /* fn_80aa0: calls fn_80b3b, fn_12a6d0 */
    fn_80aa0(ptr_2 + 8, v_3, 1, 1, 1);
    ptr_1 = v_5;
    v_3 = *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24);
  }
  ((u8 *)*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 16))[v_3] = 123;
  *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 24) = (v_3 + 1);
  *(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 32) = (*(u64 *)(ptr_2 + 32) + 1);
  slot_0 = ptr_1;
  slot_8 = 1;
  /* fn_15bf60: calls fn_15bfdc, fn_15c049, fn_80aa0 */
  unk64 v_4 = fn_15bf60(&slot_0, "elapsed", 7, arg_0 + 48);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    /* ... */
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches", 8, arg_0);
  if (v_4 != 0) {
    /* ... */
  }
  /* fn_158e60: calls fn_158eda, fn_158f46, fn_80aa0 */
  v_4 = fn_158e60(&slot_0, "searches_with_match", 19, arg_0 + 8); /* @xref_slice_target */
  /* ... */
}
stderr
xref: load 2.3ms, total 8.6ms

--only-paths-to ADDR keeps only the basic blocks from which ADDR can be reached, here the call that serializes searches_with_match. The target is marked /* @xref_slice_target */, branches that cannot lead to it are reduced to /* ... */, and everything after it is dropped, which makes long functions readable when you care about one call.

Several functions to files

Command
$ xref -b rg c 0x1835f0 0x183750 --out out
Output
out/0x1835f0.c  2146 bytes  5.5ms
out/0x183750.c  1977 bytes  6.0ms
stderr
xref: load 2.4ms, total 10.7ms

With --out DIR each function goes to DIR/<start>.c, decompiled in parallel; stdout lists the files, sizes and times. Without --out, several addresses are printed one after another.

Limits

  • Types are inferred from how values are used, not recovered from debug information; unk64 means the code does not constrain the type.
  • Instructions the lifter does not model are kept as /* 0xADDR: … */ assembly comments, never silently dropped. Cross-check critical code with xref asm.
  • Control flow the structurer cannot express without goto uses skip flags; --goto keeps the original labels instead.

Provenance

Recorded with a development build of xref after 0.4.0 on Linux x86-64, on rg = ripgrep 14.1.1 (official stripped release). Output is unchanged; long outputs are cut where marked. <!-- /xref -->
